chapters.title: Ind AS Framework, Ind AS 1 and Ind AS 8
chapters.summary: The Conceptual Framework, how Ind AS 1 shapes the financial statements, and how Ind AS 8 treats changes in policy, changes in estimate and prior period errors.
chapters.lawAsOf: Ind AS as notified by MCA, up to November 2026

lesson.heading: The Conceptual Framework and the Ind AS hierarchy
lesson.body:
The Conceptual Framework for Financial Reporting under Ind AS is not an Ind AS. It does not override any standard. It helps preparers develop a policy when no Ind AS applies (Ind AS 8 hierarchy) and helps readers understand the standards.

Key ideas you need for the exam:

- **Objective**: provide useful financial information to existing and potential investors, lenders and other creditors for decisions about providing resources.
- **Fundamental qualitative characteristics**: relevance (including materiality) and faithful representation.
- **Enhancing characteristics**: comparability, verifiability, timeliness and understandability.
- **Elements**: asset (a present economic resource controlled as a result of past events), liability (a present obligation to transfer an economic resource as a result of past events), equity, income and expenses.
- **Going concern** is the underlying assumption.

Ind AS 8 hierarchy when no Ind AS applies: management uses judgement to develop a relevant and reliable policy, referring first to Ind AS dealing with similar issues, then to the Framework. It may also consider the most recent IASB pronouncements and accepted industry practice, to the extent they do not conflict with the first two sources.

lesson.heading: Ind AS 1: complete set and structure
lesson.body:
A complete set of financial statements under Ind AS 1 comprises:

| Component | Note |
| --- | --- |
| Balance sheet at the end of the period | Called balance sheet in the Indian version |
| Statement of profit and loss for the period | Single statement: profit or loss section plus OCI section |
| Statement of changes in equity | Opening to closing reconciliation of each component |
| Statement of cash flows | Prepared under Ind AS 7 |
| Notes | Material accounting policy information and other explanations |
| Comparative information | For the preceding period |
| Balance sheet at the beginning of the preceding period | Only when a retrospective policy, restatement or reclassification has a material effect on it |

Points that are often examined:

- **Current vs non-current**: a liability is current if it is due within 12 months after the reporting period, held for trading, settled in the normal operating cycle, or the entity does not have the right at the end of the reporting period to defer settlement for at least 12 months.
- **Indian carve-out on covenant breach**: under Ind AS 1 as notified, if a long-term loan arrangement is breached on or before the reporting date and the lender agrees after the reporting period, but before approval of the financial statements, not to demand payment, the liability is not classified as current.
- **OCI** is split into items that will not be reclassified to profit or loss (remeasurement of defined benefit plans, revaluation surplus, FVOCI equity instruments) and items that may be reclassified (foreign operation translation, cash flow hedges, FVOCI debt instruments).
- No item may be presented as **extraordinary**, either in the statement of profit and loss or in the notes.
- After the 2023 amendment, entities disclose **material accounting policy information** instead of significant accounting policies.
- Schedule III Division II to the Companies Act, 2013 gives the format Indian companies use for Ind AS financial statements.

lesson.heading: Ind AS 8: policy, estimate or error
lesson.body:
The first exam step is classification. The treatment follows from it.

| Item | Meaning | Treatment |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Change in accounting policy | Change in principles, bases, conventions, rules or practices (for example, inventory cost formula FIFO to weighted average) | Retrospective, unless a new Ind AS has its own transition rule |
| Change in accounting estimate | Change in a monetary amount subject to measurement uncertainty (useful life, residual value, depreciation method, ECL, warranty provision) | Prospective: current period and future periods |
| Prior period error | Omission or misstatement in earlier periods from failure to use reliable information that was available | Retrospective restatement of comparatives and opening balances of the earliest period presented |

After the 2023 amendment, an accounting estimate is defined as a monetary amount in the financial statements that is subject to measurement uncertainty. A change in a measurement technique or input is a change in estimate unless it results from correcting an error.

A change in depreciation method is a change in estimate (Ind AS 16 para 61), not a change in policy. When it is difficult to tell whether a change is a policy change or an estimate change, treat it as a change in estimate.

If retrospective application or restatement is impracticable for a period, apply it from the earliest date that is practicable.

lesson.heading: Worked example: correcting a prior period error
lesson.body:
Kirti Ltd prepares financial statements for 2025-26 with 2024-25 comparatives. In 2025-26 it finds that depreciation of ₹2,00,000 on a machine for 2024-25 was omitted. Tax rate 25%; the tax effect is a deferred tax adjustment.

Restatement in the 2025-26 financial statements:

| Item | 2024-25 as reported (₹) | Correction (₹) | 2024-25 restated (₹) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Depreciation | 10,00,000 | 2,00,000 | 12,00,000 |
| Tax expense | 15,00,000 | (50,000) | 14,50,000 |
| Profit for the year | 45,00,000 | (1,50,000) | 43,50,000 |

Opening retained earnings of 2025-26 (that is, at 1 April 2025) fall by ₹1,50,000. The 2025-26 profit is not touched by this correction.

Journal entry in 2025-26:

| Particulars | Dr (₹) | Cr (₹) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Retained earnings (opening) | 1,50,000 | |
| Deferred tax liability | 50,000 | |
| To Accumulated depreciation | | 2,00,000 |

Disclose the nature of the error, the amount of correction for each line item and for basic and diluted EPS, and the correction at the beginning of the earliest period presented.

lesson.heading: Common mistakes
lesson.body:
- Treating a change in depreciation method or useful life as a change in policy. Both are estimates and are applied prospectively.
- Passing the correction of a prior period error through current year profit. It goes to opening retained earnings and comparatives are restated.
- Forgetting the third balance sheet when a restatement materially affects the opening balance sheet of the preceding period.
- Classifying a loan as current after a covenant breach without checking the Indian carve-out on a waiver received after the reporting date.
- Presenting a large unusual loss as extraordinary. Ind AS 1 prohibits it; disclose it separately as an exceptional item if material.

keyPoints: Fundamental qualitative characteristics: relevance and faithful representation. Going concern is the underlying assumption.

Complete set (Ind AS 1): balance sheet, statement of profit and loss (with OCI), SOCE, cash flow statement, notes, comparatives, plus a third balance sheet when a material retrospective change affects it.
Policy change and prior period error: retrospective. Estimate change: prospective.
Change in depreciation method, useful life or residual value is a change in estimate (Ind AS 16 para 61).
Indian carve-out: covenant breach waived after the reporting date but before approval keeps the loan non-current.
No extraordinary items. Disclose material accounting policy information (2023 amendment).

cases.title: Case: Vardhan Polymers Ltd
cases.body:
Vardhan Polymers Ltd prepares Ind AS financial statements for the year ended 31 March 2026 with one year of comparatives. The board approves them on 25 May 2026. Ignore tax.

- (i) In August 2025 the company found that closing inventory at 31 March 2025 was overstated by ₹6,00,000 because of a counting error. The 2024-25 financial statements have already been issued.
- (ii) From 1 April 2025 the company changed the depreciation method of its extrusion plant from written down value to straight line because the pattern of consumption of benefits has changed.
- (iii) From 1 April 2025 it changed the cost formula for raw material inventory from FIFO to weighted average, as weighted average gives more relevant information. The effect on earlier periods can be determined.
- (iv) A term loan of ₹40 crore repayable in 2030 contains a covenant on the debt-equity ratio. The covenant was breached on 28 February 2026, making the loan repayable on demand. On 15 April 2026 the bank agreed in writing not to demand repayment because of the breach.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is NOT part of a complete set of financial statements under Ind AS 1?
options: Statement of changes in equity
Board's report
Notes containing material accounting policy information
Comparative information for the preceding period
questions.explanation: The Board's report is required by the Companies Act, 2013 but is not a component of financial statements under Ind AS 1. The SOCE, notes and comparatives are all part of the complete set.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is a change in accounting estimate under Ind AS 8?
options: Revising the useful life of a machine from 10 years to 8 years
Changing the inventory cost formula from FIFO to weighted average
Correcting depreciation that was omitted in the previous year
Adopting a new Ind AS that requires retrospective application
questions.explanation: Useful life is a monetary estimate subject to measurement uncertainty, so a revision is a change in estimate applied prospectively. A change in cost formula is a policy change, an omission is a prior period error, and a new Ind AS follows its own transition provisions.

questions.prompt: Ind AS 1 allows a material loss from an earthquake to be presented as an extraordinary item in the notes, though not on the face of the statement of profit and loss.
questions.explanation: Ind AS 1 prohibits presenting any item of income or expense as extraordinary, either in the statement of profit and loss or in the notes. A material item is disclosed separately by nature and amount.

questions.prompt: Select the OCI items that will NOT be reclassified to profit or loss.
options: Remeasurement gains and losses on defined benefit plans
Revaluation surplus on property, plant and equipment
Fair value changes of equity instruments designated at FVOCI
Exchange differences on translating a foreign operation
Effective portion of a cash flow hedge
questions.explanation: Defined benefit remeasurements (Ind AS 19), revaluation surplus (Ind AS 16) and FVOCI equity gains (Ind AS 109) are never recycled. Foreign operation translation differences are recycled on disposal (Ind AS 21) and cash flow hedge reserves are recycled when the hedged item affects profit or loss.

questions.prompt: Fill the blank: Ind AS 1 requires a balance sheet as at the beginning of the ___ period when a retrospective restatement has a material effect on it.
questions.explanation: The third balance sheet is at the beginning of the preceding (comparative) period, for example 1 April 2024 in financial statements for 2025-26.

questions.prompt: While preparing 2025-26 financial statements, an entity finds that depreciation of ₹2,00,000 for 2024-25 was omitted. The tax rate is 25% and the tax effect is a deferred tax adjustment. By how much will retained earnings at 1 April 2025 be reduced? Answer in ₹.
questions.explanation:
Error correction is retrospective, net of tax.

| Particulars | ₹ |
| --- | --- |
| Omitted depreciation | 2,00,000 |
| Less: deferred tax effect at 25% | (50,000) |
| **Reduction in opening retained earnings** | **1,50,000** |

questions.prompt: A machine costing ₹12,00,000 was depreciated straight line over 10 years with nil residual value. At the start of year 5 its remaining useful life is revised to 4 years. Compute the depreciation for year 5 in ₹.
questions.explanation:
A change in useful life is a change in estimate, applied prospectively.

| Particulars | ₹ |
| --- | --- |
| Cost | 12,00,000 |
| Less: depreciation for 4 years (1,20,000 x 4) | (4,80,000) |
| Carrying amount at start of year 5 | 7,20,000 |
| Depreciation for year 5 (7,20,000 / 4) | **1,80,000** |

questions.prompt: For item (i), by how much will the 2024-25 profit be reduced when the comparatives are restated in the 2025-26 financial statements? Answer in ₹.
questions.explanation: Overstated closing inventory at 31 March 2025 overstated 2024-25 profit by ₹6,00,000. The restated 2024-25 profit falls by ₹6,00,000 and the 31 March 2025 inventory and retained earnings are reduced by the same amount. Opening balances at 1 April 2024 are not affected because the error arose in 2024-25.

questions.prompt: How should item (ii) be accounted for?
options: As a change in accounting estimate, applied prospectively from 1 April 2025
As a change in accounting policy, applied retrospectively
As a prior period error, with comparatives restated
No accounting effect; disclose only
questions.explanation: Ind AS 16 para 61 treats a change in depreciation method as a change in accounting estimate under Ind AS 8, so it is applied prospectively.

questions.prompt: How should item (iii) be accounted for?
options: Retrospectively as a change in accounting policy, adjusting opening balances of the earliest period presented
Prospectively as a change in accounting estimate
As a prior period error
Through OCI in the current year
questions.explanation: A change in cost formula is a change in accounting policy. It is voluntary and gives more relevant information, so Ind AS 8 permits it and requires retrospective application, as the effect is determinable.

questions.prompt: How should the term loan in item (iv) be classified in the balance sheet at 31 March 2026 under Ind AS 1 as notified in India?
options: Non-current, because the bank agreed before approval of the financial statements not to demand payment
Current, because the waiver came after the reporting date
Split equally between current and non-current
As equity until the waiver is formally recorded
questions.explanation: Ind AS 1 para 74 (Indian carve-out from IAS 1) says a loan in breach at the reporting date is not classified as current if the lender agrees, after the reporting period and before approval of the financial statements, not to demand payment because of the breach. Under IAS 1 the waiver would have to exist at the reporting date.

questions.prompt: In 2025-26, Saral Ltd finds that a machine costing ₹8,00,000, bought on 1 April 2024, was charged to repairs in 2024-25. The machine has a useful life of 4 years with nil residual value (straight line). Ignore tax. Show how the error is corrected in the 2025-26 financial statements, with the journal entry and the restated figures.
questions.answer:
This is a prior period error. Correct it retrospectively (Ind AS 8 para 42): restate the 2024-25 comparatives and adjust opening retained earnings of 2025-26.

Effect on 2024-25 (restated comparatives):

| Particulars | ₹ |
| --- | --- |
| Repairs expense wrongly charged, now reversed | 8,00,000 |
| Less: depreciation for 2024-25 (8,00,000 / 4) | (2,00,000) |
| **Increase in 2024-25 profit** | **6,00,000** |

Journal entries in 2025-26:

| Particulars | Dr (₹) | Cr (₹) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Plant and machinery | 8,00,000 | |
| To Accumulated depreciation | | 2,00,000 |
| To Retained earnings (opening) | | 6,00,000 |
| (Correction of prior period error) | | |
| Depreciation expense | 2,00,000 | |
| To Accumulated depreciation | | 2,00,000 |
| (Depreciation for 2025-26) | | |

Balance sheet: carrying amount ₹6,00,000 at 31 March 2025 (restated) and ₹4,00,000 at 31 March 2026.

Disclosures: nature of the error, the amount of correction for each line item and for basic and diluted EPS for 2024-25, and the correction at the start of the earliest period presented. If the effect on the 1 April 2024 balance sheet were material, a third balance sheet would be needed; here the opening 1 April 2024 balances are not affected.

questions.prompt: Distinguish between a change in accounting policy, a change in accounting estimate and correction of a prior period error under Ind AS 8, with one example of each.
questions.answer:
- Accounting policies are the specific principles, bases, conventions, rules and practices applied in preparing financial statements. A change is allowed only if required by an Ind AS or if it gives reliable and more relevant information. It is applied retrospectively unless transition provisions say otherwise. Example: inventory cost formula changed from FIFO to weighted average.
- An accounting estimate is a monetary amount subject to measurement uncertainty (2023 definition). A change results from new information or developments and is applied prospectively in the current and future periods. Examples: useful life, residual value, depreciation method, ECL allowance.
- A prior period error is an omission or misstatement arising from failure to use reliable information that was available when the earlier financial statements were approved. It is corrected by retrospective restatement of comparatives and opening balances. Example: depreciation omitted last year.
- When a change cannot be classified clearly as a policy or estimate change, it is treated as a change in estimate.

questions.prompt: Explain the going concern assessment required by Ind AS 1 and what must be disclosed when material uncertainties exist.
questions.answer:
- Ind AS 1 requires management to assess the entity's ability to continue as a going concern when preparing financial statements, considering information about at least twelve months from the end of the reporting period.
- Financial statements are prepared on a going concern basis unless management intends to liquidate or cease trading, or has no realistic alternative.
- When management is aware of material uncertainties about events or conditions that may cast significant doubt on going concern, it discloses those uncertainties.
- If the financial statements are not prepared on a going concern basis, the entity discloses that fact, the basis used and the reason.
- Under Ind AS 10, deterioration after the reporting period that shows the going concern assumption is no longer appropriate requires a change in the basis of accounting, not just a disclosure.

chapters.title: Ind AS 115: Revenue from Contracts with Customers
chapters.summary: The five-step model, variable consideration, allocation on stand-alone selling prices, over-time recognition and contract costs, with journal entries.
chapters.lawAsOf: Ind AS as notified by MCA, up to November 2026

lesson.heading: The five-step model
lesson.body:
Ind AS 115 recognises revenue when (or as) control of goods or services passes to the customer, at the amount the entity expects to be entitled to.

| Step | What you decide | Exam pointers |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1. Identify the contract | Approved, rights and payment terms identifiable, commercial substance, collection probable | Combine contracts entered at or near the same time with the same customer if negotiated as a package |
| 2. Identify performance obligations | Each distinct good or service (or series) | Distinct = capable of being distinct AND distinct in the context of the contract |
| 3. Determine the transaction price | Fixed plus variable consideration, financing, non-cash consideration, consideration payable to customer | Exclude amounts collected for third parties, such as GST |
| 4. Allocate the price | On relative stand-alone selling prices (SSP) | Estimate SSP by adjusted market, expected cost plus margin or residual approach (residual only in limited cases) |
| 5. Recognise revenue | Over time or at a point in time | Over time if any one of the three criteria in para 35 is met |

lesson.heading: Transaction price: variable consideration and financing
lesson.body:
**Variable consideration** (discounts, rebates, refunds, price concessions, incentives, bonuses, penalties) is estimated using either the expected value (many similar contracts) or the most likely amount (two possible outcomes). It is included only to the extent it is highly probable that a significant reversal of cumulative revenue will not occur when the uncertainty is resolved (the constraint).

**Significant financing component**: if payment timing gives the customer or the entity a significant financing benefit, adjust the promised amount for the time value of money. Practical expedient: ignore it if the gap between transfer and payment is one year or less.

Example: goods transferred today for ₹12,10,000 payable after 2 years; discount rate 10%.

| Particulars | ₹ |
| --- | --- |
| Revenue on delivery (12,10,000 / 1.21) | 10,00,000 |
| Interest income year 1 (10% of 10,00,000) | 1,00,000 |
| Interest income year 2 (10% of 11,00,000) | 1,10,000 |

**Right of return**: recognise revenue only for goods not expected to be returned, a refund liability for expected returns and an asset for the right to recover goods (at former carrying amount less expected recovery costs).

lesson.heading: Over time or at a point in time
lesson.body:
Revenue is recognised over time if any one of these is met (para 35):

- The customer simultaneously receives and consumes the benefits as the entity performs (for example, routine cleaning services).
- The entity's performance creates or enhances an asset the customer controls (for example, construction on the customer's land).
- The performance does not create an asset with an alternative use to the entity and the entity has an enforceable right to payment for performance completed to date.

Progress is measured by an output method (surveys, milestones, units delivered) or an input method (costs incurred, labour hours). Under the cost-to-cost input method, exclude costs that do not depict progress, such as wasted materials.

Example: contract price ₹50,00,000, total estimated cost ₹40,00,000, cost incurred to date ₹16,00,000.

| Particulars | ₹ |
| --- | --- |
| Progress (16,00,000 / 40,00,000) | 40% |
| Revenue to date (40% x 50,00,000) | 20,00,000 |
| Cost recognised | 16,00,000 |
| Profit recognised | 4,00,000 |

If the expected total cost exceeds the price, the contract is onerous and the expected loss is provided under Ind AS 37.

Otherwise, revenue is recognised at the point control transfers. Indicators: present right to payment, legal title, physical possession, risks and rewards of ownership, customer acceptance.

lesson.heading: Contract costs, contract balances and presentation
lesson.body:
- **Incremental costs of obtaining a contract** (for example, a sales commission payable only if the contract is won) are recognised as an asset if expected to be recovered. Practical expedient: expense them if the amortisation period would be one year or less.
- **Costs to fulfil a contract** not covered by another standard are capitalised if they relate directly to the contract, generate or enhance resources and are expected to be recovered.
- **Contract asset**: right to consideration conditional on something other than the passage of time. **Receivable**: unconditional right. **Contract liability**: consideration received (or due) before transfer of goods or services.
- **Principal vs agent**: a principal controls the good or service before transfer and reports revenue gross; an agent reports only its commission (net).
- **Licences**: a right to access intellectual property is recognised over time; a right to use it as it exists at the grant date is recognised at a point in time.

lesson.heading: Common mistakes
lesson.body:
- Allocating a bundle discount only to the item with the lowest margin. Unless the criteria for allocating a discount to specific obligations are met, allocate it proportionately on SSP.
- Including GST collected in the transaction price.
- Recognising the full price of a sale with a right of return as revenue and ignoring the refund liability.
- Using costs of wasted materials or uninstalled goods in a cost-to-cost percentage.
- Ignoring the constraint on variable consideration when a bonus depends on factors outside the entity's influence.

keyPoints: Five steps: contract, performance obligations, transaction price, allocation, recognition.
Distinct = capable of being distinct and distinct within the context of the contract.
Variable consideration: expected value or most likely amount, subject to the highly probable no significant reversal constraint.
Over time if any one of three criteria (para 35) is met; otherwise at a point in time when control passes.
Ignore financing component if transfer and payment are within one year (practical expedient).
Incremental cost of obtaining a contract is capitalised; expense if amortisation period is one year or less.

cases.title: Case: Nimbus Software Ltd
cases.body:
On 1 October 2025 Nimbus Software Ltd signs a contract with Orbit Retail Ltd for ₹18,00,000 (excluding GST), received in full on signing. The contract includes:

| Promise | Stand-alone selling price (₹) | Timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Software licence (right to use the software as it exists on 1 October 2025) | 12,00,000 | Licence key delivered 1 October 2025 |
| Installation (a standard service other vendors also provide; no significant customisation) | 3,00,000 | Completed 31 October 2025 |
| Technical support for 24 months | 5,00,000 | Evenly from 1 October 2025 |

Nimbus prepares financial statements to 31 March each year. Each promise is distinct.

questions.prompt: Under the five-step model of Ind AS 115, which step comes immediately after identifying the performance obligations?
options: Determine the transaction price
Allocate the transaction price
Identify the contract with the customer
Recognise revenue when a performance obligation is satisfied
questions.explanation: The order is: identify the contract, identify performance obligations, determine the transaction price, allocate it, then recognise revenue.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is NOT one of the criteria in Ind AS 115 for recognising revenue over time?
options: The customer simultaneously receives and consumes the benefits as the entity performs
The entity's performance creates or enhances an asset that the customer controls
The asset has no alternative use and the entity has an enforceable right to payment for performance to date
The customer has paid at least half of the contract price in advance
questions.explanation: Advance payment is not a criterion. Para 35 has only the three criteria listed in the other options; meeting any one of them means revenue is recognised over time.

questions.prompt: An entity may expense a sales commission paid for winning a contract if the amortisation period of the resulting asset would be one year or less.
questions.explanation: Incremental costs of obtaining a contract are normally capitalised, but Ind AS 115 para 94 gives a practical expedient to expense them when the amortisation period is one year or less.

questions.prompt: Which of the following are forms of variable consideration under Ind AS 115?
options: Volume rebates
Performance bonus for early completion
Expected price concessions
A fixed annual fee paid in advance
questions.explanation: Rebates, bonuses and price concessions make the amount uncertain, so they are variable consideration. A fixed fee paid in advance is fixed consideration (though a large advance may raise a financing component question).

questions.prompt: Fill the blank: variable consideration is included in the transaction price only to the extent it is highly probable that a significant ___ in the amount of cumulative revenue recognised will not occur.
questions.explanation: This is the constraint on variable consideration (Ind AS 115 para 56). It prevents recognising revenue that is likely to be reversed later.

questions.prompt: A builder has a contract for ₹50,00,000 that meets the over-time criteria. Estimated total cost is ₹40,00,000 and cost incurred to date (all of which depicts progress) is ₹16,00,000. Using the cost-to-cost method, compute cumulative revenue to date in ₹.

A supplier sells a product at ₹100 per unit. If the customer buys more than 1,000 units in the year, the price for all units becomes ₹90 retrospectively. Based on past experience the supplier concludes it is highly probable the customer will cross 1,000 units. In quarter 1 it sells 300 units. Compute revenue for quarter 1 in ₹.
questions.explanation:
The volume rebate is variable consideration. Since the customer is expected to cross the threshold, the transaction price is ₹90 per unit.

| Particulars | ₹ |
| --- | --- |
| Revenue = 300 x 90 | **27,000** |
| Cash or receivable = 300 x 100 | 30,000 |
| Refund liability | 3,000 |

questions.prompt: Goods are delivered today. The customer will pay ₹12,10,000 in one lump sum after 2 years. The rate that reflects a separate financing transaction with this customer is 10% p.a. Compute the revenue recognised on delivery in ₹.
questions.explanation:
There is a significant financing component (payment more than one year after transfer).

| Particulars | ₹ |
| --- | --- |
| Revenue = 12,10,000 / (1.10)^2 | **10,00,000** |
| Interest income year 1 = 10% x 10,00,000 | 1,00,000 |
| Interest income year 2 = 10% x 11,00,000 | 1,10,000 |

questions.prompt: How many performance obligations does the Nimbus contract contain?
options: Three
One
Two: licence with installation, and support
Four, counting the advance payment
questions.explanation: The licence, installation and support are each distinct: installation is a standard service other vendors provide and does not significantly modify the software, so each is a separate performance obligation. Receiving an advance is not a promise to the customer.

questions.prompt: How much of the transaction price is allocated to the software licence?
questions.explanation: Total SSP = 12,00,000 + 3,00,000 + 5,00,000 = 20,00,000. The ₹2,00,000 discount is allocated proportionately: licence = 18,00,000 x 12/20 = ₹10,80,000 (installation ₹2,70,000, support ₹4,50,000).

questions.prompt: Compute the total revenue Nimbus recognises from this contract for the year ended 31 March 2026, in ₹.
questions.explanation:
| Performance obligation | Allocated (₹) | Recognised in 2025-26 (₹) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Licence (point in time, 1 Oct 2025) | 10,80,000 | 10,80,000 |
| Installation (completed 31 Oct 2025) | 2,70,000 | 2,70,000 |
| Support (6 of 24 months) | 4,50,000 | 1,12,500 |
| **Total** | 18,00,000 | **14,62,500** |

questions.prompt: What contract liability will Nimbus show at 31 March 2026?
options: Nil
questions.explanation: The full ₹18,00,000 was received upfront and revenue of ₹14,62,500 has been recognised. The balance ₹3,37,500 (18 remaining months of support: 4,50,000 x 18/24) is a contract liability.

questions.prompt: On 15 March 2026, Rhea Appliances Ltd sells 1,000 mixers at ₹500 each for cash. Each mixer cost ₹300. Customers may return unused mixers within 30 days for a full refund. Based on experience, Rhea expects 5% to be returned, the estimate is reliable and returned mixers can be resold at a profit. Pass journal entries at the date of sale under Ind AS 115.
questions.answer:
Revenue is recognised only for mixers not expected to be returned (950 units). A refund liability is recognised for the expected returns and an asset for the right to recover the goods.

| Particulars | Dr (₹) | Cr (₹) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Bank (1,000 x 500) | 5,00,000 | |
| To Revenue from operations (950 x 500) | | 4,75,000 |
| To Refund liability (50 x 500) | | 25,000 |
| (Sale with right of return) | | |
| Cost of goods sold (950 x 300) | 2,85,000 | |
| Right to recover returned goods (50 x 300) | 15,000 | |
| To Inventory (1,000 x 300) | | 3,00,000 |
| (Cost of goods transferred) | | |

At each reporting date the estimate of returns is updated; changes adjust revenue and the refund liability. The asset is tested for impairment and presented separately from the refund liability (no netting).

questions.prompt: How does an entity decide whether it is a principal or an agent under Ind AS 115, and what is the effect on revenue?
questions.answer:
- First identify the specified good or service to be provided to the customer.
- The entity is a principal if it controls that good or service before it is transferred to the customer; it then recognises revenue gross for the consideration it expects.
- It is an agent if its obligation is to arrange for another party to provide the good or service; it recognises revenue net, as the fee or commission it keeps.
- Indicators of control (para B37): the entity is primarily responsible for fulfilling the promise, bears inventory risk before or after transfer, and has discretion in setting the price.
- Credit risk is no longer an indicator under Ind AS 115.
- Example: an online marketplace that only arranges sales by third-party sellers is an agent and reports its commission as revenue.

chapters.title: Ind AS 116: Leases
chapters.summary: Identifying a lease, the lessee's right-of-use model, lessor classification and sale and leaseback, with full lease liability workings.
chapters.lawAsOf: Ind AS as notified by MCA, up to November 2026

lesson.heading: Is there a lease?
lesson.body:
A contract is, or contains, a lease if it conveys the right to control the use of an identified asset for a period of time in exchange for consideration.

- **Identified asset**: explicitly or implicitly specified. There is no identified asset if the supplier has a substantive substitution right (practical ability to substitute and economic benefit from doing so). A capacity portion (for example, 30% of a pipeline) is not an identified asset unless it is physically distinct or represents substantially all the capacity.
- **Right to control**: the customer has the right to obtain substantially all the economic benefits from use, and the right to direct how and for what purpose the asset is used.

Lease term = non-cancellable period plus periods covered by an extension option the lessee is reasonably certain to exercise and a termination option it is reasonably certain not to exercise.

lesson.heading: Lessee accounting: single model
lesson.body:
At commencement the lessee recognises a right-of-use (ROU) asset and a lease liability, except for elected short-term leases (12 months or less, no purchase option) and leases of low-value assets.

**Lease liability** = present value of unpaid lease payments, discounted at the rate implicit in the lease or, if not readily determinable, the lessee's incremental borrowing rate. Lease payments include fixed payments (less incentives receivable), variable payments that depend on an index or rate, amounts expected under residual value guarantees, a purchase option price if reasonably certain to be exercised and termination penalties if the lease term reflects termination. Variable payments linked to sales or usage are excluded and expensed.

**ROU asset** at cost:

| Component | Sign |
| --- | --- |
| Initial measurement of lease liability | + |
| Lease payments made at or before commencement, less lease incentives received | + / - |
| Initial direct costs of the lessee | + |
| Estimated cost of dismantling and restoration (Ind AS 37) | + |

Subsequently the liability is measured at amortised cost (interest on opening balance, less payments) and the ROU asset is depreciated: over the shorter of lease term and useful life, or over useful life if ownership transfers or a purchase option is reasonably certain.

lesson.heading: Worked example: five-year lease
lesson.body:
Lease from 1 April 2025, 5 annual payments of ₹5,00,000 in arrears, incremental borrowing rate 10% (annuity factor 3.7908). No initial direct costs.

Lease liability and ROU asset = 5,00,000 x 3.7908 = ₹18,95,393 (exact discounting).

| Year | Opening (₹) | Interest 10% (₹) | Payment (₹) | Closing (₹) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 2025-26 | 18,95,393 | 1,89,539 | 5,00,000 | 15,84,932 |
| 2026-27 | 15,84,932 | 1,58,493 | 5,00,000 | 12,43,425 |

Depreciation = 18,95,393 / 5 = ₹3,79,079 a year. The total charge in year 1 (₹5,68,618) exceeds the cash rent of ₹5,00,000: Ind AS 116 front-loads expense.

At 31 March 2026 the liability splits into current ₹3,41,507 (the principal in the next payment: 5,00,000 - 1,58,493) and non-current ₹12,43,425.

lesson.heading: Lessor accounting and sale and leaseback
lesson.body:
A lessor still classifies each lease as a **finance lease** (transfers substantially all risks and rewards incidental to ownership) or an **operating lease**. Indicators of a finance lease: ownership transfers at the end, a bargain purchase option, lease term for the major part of economic life, PV of lease payments amounts to substantially all of fair value, specialised asset.

- Finance lease: derecognise the asset, recognise a receivable equal to the net investment in the lease and earn finance income at a constant periodic rate.
- Operating lease: keep the asset, depreciate it and recognise lease income on a straight-line basis.

**Sale and leaseback**: first check whether the transfer is a sale under Ind AS 115.

- If it is a sale, the seller-lessee measures the ROU asset at the proportion of the previous carrying amount that relates to the right of use retained, and recognises gain only on the rights transferred to the buyer-lessor. The 2024 amendment (notified by MCA) also requires the seller-lessee to measure the leaseback liability so that no gain arises on the right of use it retains.
- If it is not a sale, the seller keeps the asset and records the proceeds as a financial liability under Ind AS 109.

Example: carrying amount ₹6,00,000, sold at fair value ₹10,00,000, PV of leaseback payments ₹4,00,000. ROU = 6,00,000 x 4/10 = ₹2,40,000. Total gain ₹4,00,000; gain recognised = 4,00,000 x 6/10 = ₹2,40,000.

lesson.heading: Common mistakes
lesson.body:
- Discounting payments in advance as if they were in arrears. A payment at commencement is not part of the liability; it goes straight into the ROU asset.
- Including sales-linked variable rent in the lease liability.
- Adding lease incentives received to the ROU asset instead of deducting them.
- Depreciating the ROU asset over useful life when ownership does not transfer and no purchase option is reasonably certain.
- Showing the whole lease liability as non-current. The principal due within 12 months is current.

keyPoints: Lease = right to control the use of an identified asset for a period in exchange for consideration.
Lessee: ROU asset and lease liability for all leases except elected short-term (12 months or less, no purchase option) and low-value leases.
Discount rate: rate implicit in the lease, else the lessee's incremental borrowing rate.
ROU = liability + payments at or before commencement - incentives + initial direct costs + restoration estimate.
Lessor: finance vs operating classification remains.
Sale and leaseback that is a sale: gain only on rights transferred; ROU = carrying amount x PV of leaseback / fair value.

cases.title: Case: Kaveri Logistics Ltd
cases.body:
On 1 April 2025 Kaveri Logistics Ltd leases a warehouse for 4 years. Details:

| Item | Detail |
| --- | --- |
| Annual lease payment | ₹10,00,000, paid on 31 March each year (in arrears) |
| Rate implicit in the lease | Not readily determinable |
| Kaveri's incremental borrowing rate | 12% p.a. (4-year annuity factor 3.0373) |
| Initial direct costs paid by Kaveri | ₹50,000 |
| Lease incentive received from the lessor on 1 April 2025 | ₹1,00,000 |
| Ownership transfer or purchase option | None; useful life of warehouse 25 years |

Kaveri prepares financial statements to 31 March and depreciates on the straight-line basis.

questions.prompt: Under Ind AS 116, a short-term lease that a lessee may exempt from recognition is a lease that, at commencement:
options: Has a lease term of 12 months or less and contains no purchase option
Has a lease term of 12 months or less, even with a purchase option
Has annual payments below ₹1,00,000
Is cancellable by either party with a notice of 3 months
questions.explanation: Ind AS 116 Appendix A defines a short-term lease as one with a lease term of 12 months or less at commencement. A lease containing a purchase option is not a short-term lease.

questions.prompt: Which of these payments is EXCLUDED from the measurement of a lessee's lease liability?
options: Additional rent of 2% of the store's annual sales
Rent that increases each year in line with the consumer price index
Exercise price of a purchase option the lessee is reasonably certain to exercise
Amount expected to be payable under a residual value guarantee
questions.explanation: Variable payments linked to future sales or usage are expensed when incurred. Index-linked payments, reasonably certain purchase option prices and expected residual value guarantee amounts are included.

questions.prompt: Under Ind AS 116 a lessor continues to classify each lease as either a finance lease or an operating lease.
questions.explanation: Ind AS 116 introduced a single model for lessees only. Lessors keep the finance vs operating classification based on transfer of substantially all risks and rewards incidental to ownership.

questions.prompt: Which items are included in the initial cost of a lessee's right-of-use asset?
options: Initial measurement of the lease liability
Initial direct costs incurred by the lessee
Estimated restoration costs required by the lease, measured under Ind AS 37
Expected future rent based on usage of the asset
questions.explanation: The ROU asset includes the lease liability, payments made at or before commencement (less incentives), initial direct costs and restoration estimates. Usage-based variable rent is not part of the liability or the ROU asset.

questions.prompt: Fill the blank: if the interest rate implicit in the lease cannot be readily determined, the lessee discounts lease payments using its ___ borrowing rate.
questions.explanation: The incremental borrowing rate is the rate the lessee would pay to borrow, over a similar term and with similar security, the funds needed to obtain an asset of similar value in a similar economic environment.

questions.prompt: A lessee pays ₹5,00,000 at the end of each year for 5 years. Its incremental borrowing rate is 10% (5-year annuity factor 3.7908). Compute the initial lease liability, rounded to the nearest rupee.

Seller-lessee sells a building with a carrying amount of ₹6,00,000 to a buyer-lessor for its fair value of ₹10,00,000 and leases it back. The transfer is a sale under Ind AS 115. The PV of leaseback payments is ₹4,00,000. Compute the gain the seller-lessee recognises at the date of transfer, in ₹.
questions.explanation:
Gain is recognised only on the rights transferred to the buyer-lessor.

| Particulars | ₹ |
| --- | --- |
| Total gain (10,00,000 - 6,00,000) | 4,00,000 |
| Right of use retained (4,00,000 / 10,00,000) | 40% |
| ROU asset = 6,00,000 x 40% | 2,40,000 |
| Gain on rights transferred = 4,00,000 x 60% | **2,40,000** |

Entry: Dr Bank 10,00,000, Dr ROU asset 2,40,000; Cr Building 6,00,000, Cr Lease liability 4,00,000, Cr Gain 2,40,000.

questions.prompt: What is the initial lease liability of Kaveri at 1 April 2025 (to the nearest hundred rupees)?
questions.explanation: Lease liability = PV of the four payments only: 10,00,000 x 3.0373 = ₹30,37,300 (₹30,37,349 with exact factors). Initial direct costs and incentives affect the ROU asset, not the liability.

questions.prompt: Compute the cost of Kaveri's right-of-use asset at 1 April 2025, to the nearest rupee.
questions.explanation:
| Particulars | ₹ |
| --- | --- |
| Lease liability (exact discounting) | 30,37,349 |
| Add: initial direct costs | 50,000 |
| Less: lease incentive received | (1,00,000) |
| **ROU asset** | **29,87,349** |

With the rounded factor the answer is ₹29,87,300; both are accepted.

questions.prompt: Compute the interest expense on the lease liability for the year ended 31 March 2026, to the nearest rupee.
questions.explanation:
Interest = 12% x 30,37,349 = ₹3,64,482 (₹3,64,476 with the rounded liability).

| Particulars | ₹ |
| --- | --- |
| Opening liability | 30,37,349 |
| Add: interest at 12% | 3,64,482 |
| Less: payment on 31 March 2026 | (10,00,000) |
| Closing liability | 24,01,831 |

questions.prompt: What is the total charge to profit or loss for 2025-26 from this lease (depreciation plus interest), approximately?
questions.explanation: Depreciation = 29,87,349 / 4 = ₹7,46,837 (lease term of 4 years is shorter than useful life and ownership does not transfer). Interest = ₹3,64,482. Total = ₹11,11,319. The cash rent of ₹10,00,000 is not the expense, and depreciation must be on the adjusted ROU cost, not on the liability.

questions.prompt: Lessee Ltd takes a machine on lease from 1 April 2025 for 5 years at ₹5,00,000 payable at the end of each year. The incremental borrowing rate is 10%; there are no initial direct costs, incentives or purchase options. Pass journal entries for 2025-26 and show the balance sheet presentation of the lease liability at 31 March 2026.
questions.answer:
Lease liability = PV of 5 payments at 10% = ₹18,95,393. Depreciation = 18,95,393 / 5 = ₹3,79,079.

| Date | Particulars | Dr (₹) | Cr (₹) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 Apr 2025 | Right-of-use asset | 18,95,393 | |
| | To Lease liability | | 18,95,393 |
| 31 Mar 2026 | Finance cost (interest on lease liability) | 1,89,539 | |
| | To Lease liability | | 1,89,539 |
| 31 Mar 2026 | Lease liability | 5,00,000 | |
| | To Bank | | 5,00,000 |
| 31 Mar 2026 | Depreciation | 3,79,079 | |
| | To Accumulated depreciation on ROU asset | | 3,79,079 |

Lease liability at 31 March 2026 = 18,95,393 + 1,89,539 - 5,00,000 = ₹15,84,932.

| Presentation | ₹ |
| --- | --- |
| Current (5,00,000 less 2026-27 interest 1,58,493) | 3,41,507 |
| Non-current | 12,43,425 |
| Total | 15,84,932 |

ROU asset carrying amount = 18,95,393 - 3,79,079 = ₹15,16,314. Statement of profit and loss: depreciation ₹3,79,079 and finance cost ₹1,89,539. In the cash flow statement the principal portion (₹3,10,461) is a financing outflow and interest is classified per the entity's policy.

questions.prompt: Explain how an entity determines whether a contract contains a lease under Ind AS 116.
questions.answer:
- A contract contains a lease if it conveys the right to control the use of an identified asset for a period of time in exchange for consideration.
- Identified asset: specified explicitly or implicitly. If the supplier has a substantive right to substitute the asset throughout the period (practical ability and economic benefit), there is no identified asset. A capacity portion qualifies only if physically distinct or substantially all of the capacity.
- Right to obtain substantially all economic benefits from use during the period of use, including primary output and by-products.
- Right to direct the use: the customer decides how and for what purpose the asset is used, or those decisions are predetermined and the customer operates the asset or designed it.
- Protective rights of the supplier do not by themselves prevent the customer from having control.
- The assessment is made at inception and reassessed only if the terms and conditions change.

questions.prompt: How does a lessor account for a finance lease under Ind AS 116?
questions.answer:
- At commencement, derecognise the underlying asset and recognise a lease receivable equal to the net investment in the lease: the PV of lease payments receivable plus any unguaranteed residual value, discounted at the rate implicit in the lease.
- The lessor's initial direct costs are included in the net investment (except for manufacturer or dealer lessors).
- Finance income is recognised over the lease term at a constant periodic rate of return on the net investment; lease receipts reduce the receivable.
- A manufacturer or dealer lessor recognises selling profit at commencement: revenue at the lower of fair value and PV of lease payments at a market rate, and cost of sale net of the PV of unguaranteed residual value.
- The net investment is subject to Ind AS 109 derecognition and impairment (ECL) requirements, and estimated unguaranteed residual values are reviewed regularly.

chapters.title: Financial Instruments: Ind AS 32, 109 and 107
chapters.summary: Liability vs equity, classification of financial assets, amortised cost and effective interest, expected credit loss and derivative basics.
chapters.lawAsOf: Ind AS as notified by MCA, up to November 2026

lesson.heading: Ind AS 32: liability or equity
lesson.body:
The test is substance, not legal form. A financial liability exists when the issuer has a contractual obligation to deliver cash or another financial asset, or to exchange financial instruments on potentially unfavourable terms.

| Instrument | Classification |
| --- | --- |
| Equity shares | Equity |
| Preference shares mandatorily redeemable for cash | Liability (dividends are finance cost) |
| Non-redeemable preference shares with discretionary dividends | Equity |
| Contract settled in a variable number of own shares worth a fixed amount | Liability |
| Convertible debentures (fixed amount for fixed number of shares) | Compound: liability and equity components |

**Split accounting for a compound instrument**: liability component = PV of interest and principal at the market rate for similar debt without conversion. Equity component = proceeds minus liability. The equity component is not remeasured later.

Ind AS 107 requires disclosures about the significance of financial instruments and the nature and extent of credit, liquidity and market risks.

lesson.heading: Ind AS 109: classification of financial assets
lesson.body:
Debt instruments are classified using two tests: the **business model** for managing the assets and whether contractual cash flows are **solely payments of principal and interest (SPPI)** on the principal outstanding.

| Business model | SPPI met | Category |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Hold to collect contractual cash flows | Yes | Amortised cost |
| Hold to collect and sell | Yes | FVOCI (recycled to P&L on derecognition) |
| Other (trading, managed on fair value basis) | Any | FVTPL |
| Any | No | FVTPL |

Equity instruments are FVTPL, but for an equity investment not held for trading an entity may make an irrevocable election at initial recognition to present fair value changes in OCI. Those OCI amounts are never recycled to profit or loss (they may be moved within equity); dividends go to profit or loss.

A fair value option can designate a financial asset at FVTPL if it removes an accounting mismatch.

**Initial measurement**: fair value plus transaction costs, except for FVTPL assets where transaction costs are expensed. Trade receivables without a significant financing component are measured at transaction price.

Financial liabilities are mostly at amortised cost; held-for-trading liabilities and derivatives are at FVTPL. For a liability designated at FVTPL, fair value change due to own credit risk goes to OCI.

lesson.heading: Amortised cost and effective interest
lesson.body:
The effective interest rate (EIR) exactly discounts estimated future cash flows to the gross carrying amount. Interest income = EIR x opening amortised cost.

Example: a 3-year bond, face value ₹10,00,000, coupon 6% paid annually, bought for ₹9,48,458 (EIR 8%).

| Year | Opening (₹) | Interest at 8% (₹) | Coupon received (₹) | Closing (₹) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | 9,48,458 | 75,877 | 60,000 | 9,64,335 |
| 2 | 9,64,335 | 77,147 | 60,000 | 9,81,482 |
| 3 | 9,81,482 | 78,518 | 60,000 | 10,00,000 |

The year 3 interest is rounded so that the closing balance equals the redemption amount.

Transaction costs and premiums or discounts are spread through the EIR, not expensed.

lesson.heading: Expected credit loss and derivatives
lesson.body:
Impairment under Ind AS 109 applies to amortised cost and FVOCI debt assets, lease receivables, contract assets, loan commitments and financial guarantees. It is forward-looking.

| Stage | Condition | Loss allowance | Interest on |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | No significant increase in credit risk since initial recognition | 12-month ECL | Gross carrying amount |
| 2 | Significant increase in credit risk | Lifetime ECL | Gross carrying amount |
| 3 | Credit-impaired | Lifetime ECL | Net carrying amount (amortised cost) |

There is a rebuttable presumption that credit risk has increased significantly when payments are more than 30 days past due.

**Simplified approach**: for trade receivables and contract assets without a significant financing component, the loss allowance is always lifetime ECL, often computed with a provision matrix.

| Ageing | Gross (₹) | Loss rate | ECL (₹) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Not due | 20,00,000 | 0.5% | 10,000 |
| 1-30 days | 8,00,000 | 2% | 16,000 |
| 31-90 days | 5,00,000 | 6% | 30,000 |
| Over 90 days | 2,00,000 | 25% | 50,000 |
| **Total** | 35,00,000 | | **1,06,000** |

**Derivatives**: a financial instrument whose value changes in response to an underlying, that requires no or a smaller initial net investment, and that is settled at a future date. Derivatives are FVTPL unless designated in an effective hedge. Hedge types: fair value hedge, cash flow hedge (effective portion in OCI) and hedge of a net investment in a foreign operation.

lesson.heading: Common mistakes
lesson.body:
- Capitalising transaction costs on a FVTPL asset. They are expensed.
- Recycling FVOCI equity gains to profit or loss on sale. Only FVOCI debt instruments recycle.
- Measuring the equity component of a convertible first. The liability is measured first and equity is the residual.
- Using the coupon rate instead of the EIR for interest income at amortised cost.
- Recognising ECL only when a default happens. Ind AS 109 requires a 12-month or lifetime allowance from day one.

keyPoints: Ind AS 32: contractual obligation to deliver cash = liability. Redeemable preference shares are liabilities.
Compound instrument: liability = PV at market rate for similar non-convertible debt; equity = residual.
Debt assets: business model + SPPI decide amortised cost, FVOCI or FVTPL.
Equity FVOCI election is irrevocable and never recycled; dividends go to P&L.
ECL: stage 1 = 12-month ECL; stages 2 and 3 = lifetime ECL; trade receivables use the simplified approach.
Transaction costs: added for amortised cost and FVOCI, expensed for FVTPL.

cases.title: Case: Suryoday Investments Ltd
cases.body:
Suryoday Investments Ltd made the following investments on 1 April 2025. Its year ends on 31 March 2026.

| Investment | Details |
| --- | --- |
| (a) Delta Ltd equity shares | 10,000 shares at ₹500 each plus transaction costs of ₹10,000. A long-term strategic holding; Suryoday made the irrevocable FVOCI election. Fair value on 31 March 2026: ₹560 per share |
| (b) Gamma Ltd equity shares | 5,000 shares at ₹200 each plus transaction costs of ₹5,000. Bought for short-term trading. Fair value on 31 March 2026: ₹230 per share |
| (c) Government bonds | Fixed coupon, held to collect contractual cash flows until maturity |
| (d) Units of an open-ended equity mutual fund | Puttable units whose value depends on the fund's net asset value |

Ignore taxes and dividends.

questions.prompt: A company holds bonds whose cash flows are solely principal and interest. Its business model is to collect contractual cash flows and also to sell the bonds when liquidity needs arise. How are the bonds measured under Ind AS 109?
options: Fair value through other comprehensive income
Amortised cost
Fair value through profit or loss only
Cost less impairment
questions.explanation: A hold-to-collect-and-sell business model with SPPI cash flows leads to FVOCI. Interest (using EIR) and ECL go to profit or loss; other fair value changes go to OCI and are recycled on derecognition.

questions.prompt: A company issues 8% preference shares that must be redeemed at par after 5 years, with cumulative dividends. How are they classified by the issuer under Ind AS 32?
options: Financial liability
Equity
Compound instrument with an equity component
Provision under Ind AS 37
questions.explanation: The issuer has a contractual obligation to pay cash on redemption and to pay the cumulative dividends. So the instrument is a financial liability and the dividends are presented as finance cost.

questions.prompt: When an equity investment designated at FVOCI is sold, the cumulative gain in OCI is reclassified to profit or loss.
questions.explanation: For equity instruments designated at FVOCI, amounts in OCI are never recycled to profit or loss. The entity may transfer the cumulative gain or loss within equity, for example to retained earnings.

questions.prompt: Which characteristics are part of the Ind AS 109 definition of a derivative?
options: Its value changes in response to a specified underlying such as an interest rate, price or exchange rate
It requires no initial net investment or one smaller than for similar contracts
It is settled at a future date
It must be traded on a recognised stock exchange
questions.explanation: The three elements are an underlying, little or no initial net investment, and settlement at a future date. Over-the-counter forwards and swaps are derivatives too, so exchange trading is not required.

questions.prompt: Fill the blank: for trade receivables without a significant financing component, Ind AS 109 requires the ___ approach, under which the loss allowance is always lifetime ECL.
questions.explanation: The simplified approach avoids tracking changes in credit risk. A provision matrix based on ageing and historical loss rates, adjusted for forward-looking information, is a common practical method.

questions.prompt: Trade receivables at year end: not due ₹20,00,000 (loss rate 0.5%), 1-30 days past due ₹8,00,000 (2%), 31-90 days ₹5,00,000 (6%), over 90 days ₹2,00,000 (25%). Compute the required loss allowance in ₹.

A company buys a 3-year bond with face value ₹10,00,000 and an annual coupon of 6% for ₹9,48,458. It is held at amortised cost and the EIR is 8%. Compute the amortised cost at the end of year 1, rounded to the nearest rupee.
questions.explanation:
| Particulars | ₹ |
| --- | --- |
| Opening amortised cost | 9,48,458 |
| Add: interest income at EIR 8% | 75,877 |
| Less: coupon received (6% x 10,00,000) | (60,000) |
| **Closing amortised cost** | **9,64,335** |

questions.prompt: A company issues 3-year convertible debentures of ₹50,00,000 at par with a 5% coupon paid annually in arrears. The market rate for similar debt without a conversion option is 9%. Compute the liability component at issue, rounded to the nearest rupee (9% factors: annuity 3 years 2.5313, PV year 3 0.7722).
questions.explanation:
| Particulars | ₹ |
| --- | --- |
| PV of interest = 2,50,000 x 2.5313 | 6,32,825 |
| PV of principal = 50,00,000 x 0.7722 | 38,61,000 |
| Liability component (rounded factors) | 44,93,825 |

Exact discounting gives ₹44,93,741; both are accepted. Equity component = 50,00,000 - 44,93,741 = ₹5,06,259.

questions.prompt: Compute the fair value gain on the Delta Ltd shares recognised in OCI for 2025-26, in ₹.
questions.explanation:
For FVOCI equity, transaction costs are added to the initial carrying amount.

| Particulars | ₹ |
| --- | --- |
| Fair value at 31 March 2026 (10,000 x 560) | 56,00,000 |
| Less: initial carrying amount (50,00,000 + 10,000) | (50,10,000) |
| **Gain in OCI** | **5,90,000** |

questions.prompt: What is the net effect of the Gamma Ltd shares on profit or loss for 2025-26?
options: Net gain of ₹1,45,000
Net gain of ₹1,50,000
Net gain of ₹1,45,000 in OCI, nil in profit or loss
Net gain of ₹1,55,000
questions.explanation: Held for trading equity is FVTPL. Transaction costs of ₹5,000 are expensed on day one and the asset is recognised at ₹10,00,000. Fair value gain = 11,50,000 - 10,00,000 = ₹1,50,000. Net effect on profit = 1,50,000 - 5,000 = ₹1,45,000.

questions.prompt: How should the government bonds in (c) be measured?
options: Amortised cost
FVOCI with recycling
FVTPL
FVOCI without recycling
questions.explanation: A hold-to-collect business model and fixed coupon cash flows that are SPPI lead to amortised cost under Ind AS 109 para 4.1.2.

questions.prompt: How should the mutual fund units in (d) be classified?
options: FVTPL, because the cash flows are not solely payments of principal and interest
FVOCI, by making the equity election
Amortised cost, because they are held long term
At cost, as fair value cannot be measured
questions.explanation: Puttable units are not equity instruments of the fund from the holder's view for the FVOCI election (they meet the definition of a financial liability of the fund, presented as equity only by exception), and their returns depend on NAV, so SPPI fails. They are measured at FVTPL.

questions.prompt: On 1 April 2025 Arjun Ltd issues 50,000 convertible debentures of ₹100 each at par. Coupon 5% is payable annually on 31 March. At the end of 3 years each debenture is convertible into equity shares at the holder's option or redeemable at par. The market rate for similar debentures without conversion is 9%. Pass journal entries for 2025-26 (round to the nearest rupee).
questions.answer:
Split the compound instrument (Ind AS 32 para 28-32).

| Particulars | ₹ |
| --- | --- |
| PV of interest: 2,50,000 for 3 years at 9% | 6,32,824 |
| PV of principal: 50,00,000 / (1.09)^3 | 38,60,917 |
| Liability component | 44,93,741 (rounded) |
| Equity component (50,00,000 - 44,93,741) | 5,06,259 |

Journal entries:

| Date | Particulars | Dr (₹) | Cr (₹) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 Apr 2025 | Bank | 50,00,000 | |
| | To 5% Convertible debentures (liability) | | 44,93,741 |
| | To Equity component of compound financial instruments | | 5,06,259 |
| 31 Mar 2026 | Finance cost (9% x 44,93,741) | 4,04,437 | |
| | To 5% Convertible debentures (liability) | | 4,04,437 |
| 31 Mar 2026 | 5% Convertible debentures (liability) | 2,50,000 | |
| | To Bank | | 2,50,000 |

Liability at 31 March 2026 = 44,93,741 + 4,04,437 - 2,50,000 = ₹46,48,178. The liability accretes to ₹50,00,000 by the end of year 3. The equity component stays unchanged; on conversion the liability is transferred to equity with no gain or loss.

questions.prompt: Explain the general (three-stage) approach to expected credit loss under Ind AS 109.
questions.answer:
- ECL is a probability-weighted estimate of credit losses (PV of cash shortfalls), using reasonable and supportable information about past events, current conditions and forecasts.
- Stage 1: no significant increase in credit risk since initial recognition. Loss allowance = 12-month ECL; interest on gross carrying amount.
- Stage 2: significant increase in credit risk (rebuttable presumption at more than 30 days past due). Loss allowance = lifetime ECL; interest still on gross amount.
- Stage 3: credit-impaired (objective evidence such as default or bankruptcy; rebuttable presumption at 90 days past due for default). Lifetime ECL; interest on net carrying amount.
- Assets can move back to stage 1 if credit risk improves. The allowance change is an impairment gain or loss in profit or loss.
- The simplified approach (lifetime ECL always) applies to trade receivables and contract assets without a significant financing component, and is optional for lease receivables and those with a financing component.

lesson.heading: Ind AS 16: cost, components and revaluation
lesson.body:
PPE is recognised at cost when future economic benefits are probable and cost can be measured reliably.

| Included in cost | Excluded from cost |
| --- | --- |
| Purchase price including non-refundable duties, net of trade discounts | Recoverable GST (input tax credit) |
| Site preparation, delivery, installation and testing (proceeds from selling items produced during testing go to P&L, not against cost) | Staff training and opening a new facility |
| Professional fees | Administration and general overheads |
| Initial estimate of dismantling and restoration cost (PV, Ind AS 37) | Initial operating losses and costs after the asset is ready for use |
| Borrowing costs on a qualifying asset (Ind AS 23) | Advertising and promotion |

**Component accounting**: each part with a cost significant to the total is depreciated separately. Major inspection costs are capitalised as a component.

**Revaluation model**: applied to an entire class. Increase goes to OCI (revaluation surplus), except to the extent it reverses a decrease previously charged to profit or loss. A decrease goes to profit or loss, except to the extent of an existing surplus on the same asset. Surplus may be transferred directly to retained earnings as the asset is used or on derecognition; it is never recycled.

Depreciation method, useful life and residual value are reviewed at least at each financial year end; changes are estimates (Ind AS 8).

lesson.heading: Ind AS 38 and Ind AS 40
lesson.body:
**Intangible assets**: identifiable, non-monetary, without physical substance, controlled, with probable future benefits.

- Research phase: always expensed.
- Development phase: capitalised only when all six criteria are shown: technical feasibility, intention to complete, ability to use or sell, how it will generate probable future benefits, availability of resources, and reliable measurement of expenditure.
- Internally generated goodwill, brands, mastheads, publishing titles and customer lists are never recognised.
- Finite life: amortise over useful life. Indefinite life: no amortisation, impairment test annually and whenever there is an indication.
- The revaluation model is allowed only if there is an active market.

**Investment property** (land or building held to earn rentals or for capital appreciation, not for own use or sale in the ordinary course):

- Ind AS 40 as notified in India permits only the **cost model**; fair value must be disclosed. This is a carve-out from IAS 40, which allows a fair value model.
- Transfers in or out happen only on a change in use with evidence (for example, start of an operating lease to a third party, or start of owner occupation). Under the cost model, transfers are at carrying amount.
- A property leased to a subsidiary is investment property in the separate financial statements but PPE in the consolidated financial statements.

lesson.heading: Ind AS 36: impairment
lesson.body:
At each reporting date look for indicators of impairment. Goodwill, indefinite-life intangibles and intangibles not yet available for use are tested annually regardless.

Impairment loss = carrying amount - recoverable amount, where recoverable amount = higher of fair value less costs of disposal (FVLCD) and value in use (VIU).

Example: carrying amount ₹50,00,000, FVLCD ₹42,00,000, VIU ₹45,00,000. Recoverable amount = ₹45,00,000; impairment loss = ₹5,00,000.

**Cash-generating unit (CGU)**: the smallest identifiable group of assets generating largely independent cash inflows. Goodwill is allocated to CGUs. A CGU loss is allocated:

- first to goodwill allocated to the CGU;
- then to other assets pro rata to their carrying amounts, but no asset is reduced below the highest of its FVLCD, VIU and zero.

**Reversal**: allowed for assets other than goodwill if estimates change, up to the carrying amount (net of depreciation) that would have existed had no impairment been recognised. Impairment of goodwill is never reversed.

lesson.heading: Worked example: decommissioning cost
lesson.body:
A plant costing ₹2,00,00,000 is ready for use on 1 April 2025. Life 10 years. The entity must dismantle it at the end, at an estimated ₹50,00,000. Pre-tax discount rate 10%.

| Particulars | ₹ |
| --- | --- |
| PV of dismantling = 50,00,000 / (1.10)^10 | 19,27,716 |
| Cost of plant = 2,00,00,000 + 19,27,716 | 2,19,27,716 |
| Depreciation 2025-26 = 2,19,27,716 / 10 | 21,92,772 |
| Unwinding of discount 2025-26 = 10% x 19,27,716 (finance cost) | 1,92,772 |
| Provision at 31 March 2026 | 21,20,488 |

Under the cost model, a change in the estimated dismantling cost or discount rate adjusts the cost of the asset (Appendix A to Ind AS 16), not profit or loss, and the revised depreciable amount is spread over the remaining life.

lesson.heading: Common mistakes
lesson.body:
- Capitalising recoverable GST, training costs or general overheads.
- Using the fair value model for investment property. Ind AS 40 in India allows only the cost model.
- Allocating a CGU impairment pro rata to all assets including goodwill. Goodwill absorbs the loss first.
- Reversing a goodwill impairment when the CGU recovers.
- Treating the unwinding of a decommissioning provision as depreciation. It is a finance cost.

keyPoints: PPE cost includes PV of dismantling and restoration; excludes recoverable GST, training and admin overheads.
Revaluation increase to OCI unless reversing an earlier P&L decrease; surplus is never recycled.
Ind AS 38: research expensed; development capitalised only when all six criteria are met; internally generated brands never recognised.
Ind AS 40 (India): cost model only, fair value disclosed.
Recoverable amount = higher of FVLCD and value in use.
CGU loss: goodwill first, then pro rata; goodwill impairment is never reversed.

cases.title: Case: Meghdoot Hotels Ltd
cases.body:
Meghdoot Hotels Ltd prepares financial statements for the year ended 31 March 2026 and uses the revaluation model for land and buildings.

- (a) The carrying amount of its main hotel building at 31 March 2026, before revaluation, is ₹6,00,00,000. Its fair value is ₹6,80,00,000. In 2023-24 a revaluation decrease of ₹30,00,000 on this building was charged to profit or loss (there was no surplus then).
- (b) It owns a separate office building leased to unrelated tenants under operating leases. It is held only to earn rentals.
- (c) Its restaurant division is a CGU with these carrying amounts: goodwill ₹40,00,000, kitchen equipment ₹1,20,00,000 and furniture ₹80,00,000. Its recoverable amount is ₹1,80,00,000. Individual recoverable amounts of the equipment and furniture cannot be determined.

Ignore tax and depreciation for the year.

questions.prompt: After initial recognition, how does an Indian company measure investment property under Ind AS 40 as notified?
options: Cost model only, with fair value disclosed in the notes
Fair value model with changes in profit or loss
Either the cost model or the fair value model, as a policy choice
Revaluation model with changes in OCI
questions.explanation: Ind AS 40 removed the fair value model of IAS 40. Investment property is measured using the cost model and its fair value is disclosed.

questions.prompt: Which of the following may be recognised as an intangible asset under Ind AS 38?
options: Development cost incurred after technical feasibility and all other para 57 criteria are demonstrated
Cost of research into new materials
Cost of building an internally generated brand
Cost of a training programme for staff
questions.explanation: Development cost is capitalised once all six para 57 criteria are met. Research costs, internally generated brands and training costs are expensed.

questions.prompt: A revaluation increase is recognised in profit or loss to the extent it reverses a revaluation decrease of the same asset previously recognised in profit or loss.
questions.explanation: Ind AS 16 para 39: the increase goes to OCI, except to the extent it reverses a decrease of the same asset that was charged to profit or loss; that part is credited to profit or loss.

questions.prompt: Which of the following are included in the cost of an item of PPE under Ind AS 16?
options: Site preparation costs
Professional fees of engineers for installation
PV of the estimated cost of dismantling the asset at the end of its life
Cost of training staff to operate the machine
Initial operating losses while demand builds up
questions.explanation: Directly attributable costs and the initial dismantling estimate are capitalised. Training costs and initial operating losses are expensed (Ind AS 16 para 16-20).

questions.prompt: Fill the blank: recoverable amount is the higher of an asset's fair value less costs of disposal and its value in ___.
questions.explanation: Value in use is the PV of future cash flows expected from the asset or CGU, using a pre-tax discount rate.

questions.prompt: Compute the cost of a machine under Ind AS 16 in ₹: list price ₹40,00,000; trade discount ₹2,00,000; GST ₹6,84,000 (fully creditable); freight ₹1,00,000; installation ₹1,50,000; staff training ₹50,000; allocated administration overheads ₹30,000; PV of dismantling cost ₹2,00,000.
questions.explanation:
| Particulars | ₹ |
| --- | --- |
| List price | 40,00,000 |
| Less: trade discount | (2,00,000) |
| Freight | 1,00,000 |
| Installation | 1,50,000 |
| PV of dismantling cost | 2,00,000 |
| **Cost** | **42,50,000** |

Creditable GST, training and admin overheads are excluded.

questions.prompt: An asset has a carrying amount of ₹50,00,000. Its fair value less costs of disposal is ₹42,00,000 and its value in use is ₹45,00,000. Compute the impairment loss in ₹.
For item (a), how much of the revaluation increase is recognised in OCI for 2025-26? Answer in ₹.
questions.explanation:
| Particulars | ₹ |
| --- | --- |
| Total increase (6,80,00,000 - 6,00,00,000) | 80,00,000 |
| Less: reversal of the earlier decrease, credited to profit or loss | (30,00,000) |
| **Credited to OCI (revaluation surplus)** | **50,00,000** |

questions.prompt: How should the office building in item (b) be accounted for?
options: As investment property under the cost model, with fair value disclosed
As PPE under the revaluation model, like the other buildings
As investment property at fair value through profit or loss
As inventory held for sale
questions.explanation: A building held to earn rentals from third parties is investment property. The PPE revaluation policy does not extend to it, and Ind AS 40 in India permits only the cost model.

questions.prompt: For item (c), compute the impairment loss allocated to kitchen equipment, in ₹.
questions.explanation:
| Particulars | ₹ |
| --- | --- |
| Carrying amount of CGU (40 + 120 + 80 lakh) | 2,40,00,000 |
| Recoverable amount | 1,80,00,000 |
| Impairment loss | 60,00,000 |
| Allocated to goodwill first | 40,00,000 |
| Balance to other assets | 20,00,000 |
| Kitchen equipment share: 20,00,000 x 120/200 | **12,00,000** |
| Furniture share: 20,00,000 x 80/200 | 8,00,000 |

questions.prompt: In 2026-27 the restaurant CGU's recoverable amount rises well above its carrying amount. Which part of the 2025-26 impairment can be reversed?
options: Only the amounts allocated to equipment and furniture, subject to the depreciated carrying amount cap
The whole ₹60,00,000, including goodwill
Only the goodwill part
None; impairment losses are never reversed under Ind AS 36
questions.explanation: Ind AS 36 para 124 prohibits reversing goodwill impairment. Other assets can be written back, but not above the carrying amount they would have had (net of depreciation) without the impairment.

questions.prompt: An intangible asset is assessed as having an indefinite useful life. How is it treated after recognition?
options: Not amortised; tested for impairment annually and whenever there is an indication
Amortised over 10 years by default
Amortised over 20 years with an annual impairment test
Written off in the year of acquisition
questions.explanation: Ind AS 38 para 107-108: indefinite does not mean infinite, but no amortisation is charged. The asset is tested annually and the indefinite-life assessment is reviewed every period.

questions.prompt: Oceanic Energy Ltd commissions an offshore platform on 1 April 2025 at a cost of ₹2,00,00,000. Useful life 10 years. A licence condition requires dismantling at the end, estimated at ₹50,00,000 in 10 years' time. Pre-tax discount rate 10%. Pass journal entries for 2025-26 (round to the nearest rupee).
questions.answer:
PV of dismantling cost = 50,00,000 / (1.10)^10 = ₹19,27,716. Cost of the platform = 2,00,00,000 + 19,27,716 = ₹2,19,27,716.

| Date | Particulars | Dr (₹) | Cr (₹) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 Apr 2025 | Offshore platform (PPE) | 2,19,27,716 | |
| | To Bank | | 2,00,00,000 |
| | To Provision for decommissioning | | 19,27,716 |
| 31 Mar 2026 | Depreciation (2,19,27,716 / 10) | 21,92,772 | |
| | To Accumulated depreciation | | 21,92,772 |
| 31 Mar 2026 | Finance cost (unwinding: 10% x 19,27,716) | 1,92,772 | |
| | To Provision for decommissioning | | 1,92,772 |

At 31 March 2026: carrying amount of the platform ₹1,97,34,944; provision ₹21,20,488 (non-current). The provision grows to ₹50,00,000 by the end of year 10. A change in the estimate later adjusts the asset cost under Appendix A to Ind AS 16.

questions.prompt: State the conditions in Ind AS 38 for recognising an intangible asset arising from development, and how such an asset is measured afterwards.
questions.answer:
- Expenditure in the research phase is expensed. If research and development phases cannot be distinguished, all expenditure is treated as research.
- Development expenditure is capitalised only when the entity can demonstrate all of (para 57): technical feasibility of completing the asset; intention to complete and use or sell it; ability to use or sell it; how it will generate probable future economic benefits (a market or internal usefulness); availability of adequate technical, financial and other resources; and ability to measure the expenditure reliably.
- Only expenditure after the criteria are first met is capitalised; earlier expensed amounts are not reinstated.
- After recognition: cost model (or revaluation model only if an active market exists). Finite-life assets are amortised from when available for use; assets not yet available for use are tested for impairment annually under Ind AS 36.

chapters.title: Ind AS 37, Ind AS 10 and Ind AS 12
chapters.summary: Provisions, contingent liabilities and onerous contracts, adjusting and non-adjusting events after the reporting period, and deferred tax under the balance sheet approach.
